data.name: OneScreen Solar Sails
data.detailed_description:
Arcade multiplayer for gatherings.

Free for All, Team Game, Football, Capture the flag mods.

Party game! Up to 8 players on one screen!

Only three buttons game - turn left, turn right and fire!

Shops - you'll not lose anything at death. Buy more solar sails, canon, drill power, armor, ship's durability, cannons range...
PowerUps - temporary gain speed, drill power, cannon's range, power, piercing and frost powerups.
Meteorites drill to destroy, pickup to collect, get it to shops to get more credits.

Islands, clouds, shores, open sea settings

reviews.review:
OneScreen Solar Sails is a lightweight arcade multiplayer game that focuses on chaotic naval battles, accessible controls, and competitive entertainment. Developed and published by Anti-Ded GameDev, it embraces the simplicity of traditional party games while introducing ship upgrades, resource gathering, and several competitive objectives. Rather than attempting to deliver a realistic sailing simulation, it creates an environment where players can immediately participate in unpredictable battles. Supporting up to eight participants on a single screen, its greatest attraction is the opportunity to enjoy fast-paced competition with friends. Although its relatively basic presentation and limited mechanical complexity prevent it from becoming particularly ambitious, its straightforward approach provides an entertaining foundation for casual multiplayer sessions.

The gameplay revolves around an unusually simple three-button control system that allows players to turn left, turn right, and fire their weapons. This minimalist design makes the experience approachable even for people unfamiliar with naval combat games. However, successfully maneuvering around opponents requires more attention than the basic controls initially suggest. Players must anticipate enemy movements, position their ships effectively, and recognize opportunities to attack or retreat. The simplicity encourages immediate participation, although the restricted movement options may eventually feel limiting to players accustomed to more sophisticated arcade combat systems. Nevertheless, the controls are appropriate for a party game where accessibility and quick reactions are more important than mechanical complexity.

One of its strongest features is the selection of multiplayer modes. Free for All encourages unrestricted battles where every participant becomes a potential threat, while Team Game introduces cooperation and coordinated attacks. Football changes the competitive objective, offering a welcome alternative to conventional ship combat, whereas Capture the Flag emphasizes positioning and objective management. These different modes provide opportunities to experiment with various approaches and prevent every session from following exactly the same structure. The experience becomes particularly appealing when several players participate simultaneously, creating unpredictable encounters and amusing competitive situations. However, the enjoyment largely depends on having an enthusiastic group, since the mechanics themselves offer relatively little complexity beyond their multiplayer interactions.

The upgrade system adds meaningful progression to the otherwise straightforward gameplay. Players can visit shops to improve their ships through additional solar sails, stronger cannons, enhanced drilling capabilities, improved armor, greater durability, and increased weapon range. An especially convenient feature is that purchased improvements are retained after death, reducing the frustration of losing accumulated progress. This encourages continued participation even when players suffer repeated defeats. Choosing between offensive improvements, defensive protection, and other enhancements also introduces a modest strategic element. However, the system may create competitive imbalances when certain participants accumulate considerably stronger equipment, potentially making encounters less welcoming for newcomers.

Resource gathering provides another activity beyond attacking opponents. Players can destroy meteorites using their drills, collect the resulting materials, and deliver them to shops to earn credits. This mechanic introduces a useful relationship between exploration, resource management, and combat progression. Participants must decide whether to concentrate on collecting valuable materials or engage enemies directly. Temporary power-ups further diversify encounters by providing improvements such as additional speed, stronger drilling, extended cannon range, increased firepower, piercing attacks, and freezing effects. These bonuses can create sudden advantages and encourage players to adjust their tactics during battles. Although the systems are relatively uncomplicated, their combination gives the game more substance than its minimal controls might initially suggest.

The environmental settings include islands, clouds, coastlines, and open seas, providing different surroundings for multiplayer encounters. These locations contribute some variety to movement and positioning, although the game does not emphasize extensive exploration or elaborate environmental interactions. Its visual presentation is functional rather than impressive, prioritizing recognizable objects and readable action over detailed graphics. The modest technical requirements make it suitable for relatively inexpensive computer hardware, requiring only basic processing capabilities and limited storage space. While this accessibility is beneficial, the overall presentation lacks the visual sophistication and atmosphere associated with more polished arcade releases.

Multiplayer remains the central reason to consider the game. Shared-screen competitive and cooperative functionality allows several participants to play together, while Steam Remote Play Together provides an additional option for connecting with friends remotely. Single-player functionality is also listed, but the experience is clearly designed around social competition. Consequently, players primarily interested in solo entertainment may find the available activities insufficiently engaging over extended periods. Replayability comes mainly from experimenting with different modes, purchasing upgrades, and competing against human opponents rather than discovering substantial new content. The limited number of Steam user reviews also makes its broader reception difficult to assess confidently.

Regarding Steam Deck compatibility, OneScreen Solar Sails currently has no confirmed official Verified or Playable classification in the available Steam information, making its compatibility status Unknown or Unverified. Its low system requirements and simple controls suggest that handheld operation could be feasible, but proper functionality through Proton, controller configuration, and multiplayer performance cannot be guaranteed. Windows is the officially listed operating system, so Steam Deck owners should be prepared for possible compatibility adjustments or limitations.

Overall, OneScreen Solar Sails delivers a modest but potentially enjoyable multiplayer experience through uncomplicated naval combat, accessible controls, permanent upgrades, and varied competitive objectives. Its strongest qualities emerge when several friends participate, turning simple mechanics into entertaining battles. However, repetitive gameplay, limited depth, basic presentation, and dependence on multiplayer participation restrict its lasting appeal. It is best recommended to casual players seeking an inexpensive party game rather than those expecting a substantial naval adventure or sophisticated combat simulation.

A simple yet enjoyable arcade multiplayer experience with entertaining ship battles and worthwhile progression mechanics, held back by limited variety, modest presentation, and uncertain Steam Deck compatibility.

Rating: 6/10
